To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

medical students' moral decision making during professionalism dilemmas is influenced by the moral climate of the clinical setting, the students' perceived moral values, and their habituation or disturbance with repeated experiences of the dilemmas.
Medical students often experience and/or witness professionalism dilemmas wherein they make moral decisions.

medical students experience moral distress and burnout when their moral values are violated by organizational constraints or power differentials; they habituate to moral transgressions if they believe they are for the greater good; they can develop habits of enacting appropriate resistance behaviors when modeled; and they are more likely to develop such habits when they have been exposed to moral decision making in the context of professionalism dilemmas.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
medical educators should teach medical students about professionalism and the importance of moral decision-making in the context of professionalism dilemmas.

medical educators can facilitate students' moral reasoning by providing opportunities for students to experience and learn to resist organizational constraints and power imbalances that can result in professionalism lapses.

The main takeaway from our work is that
medical educators must be prepared to model appropriate resistance behaviors to professionalism dilemmas.
educators can facilitate students' habituated moral decision-making by helping students recognize and resist professionalism transgressions.
educators can help students develop a moral compass that will help them navigate dilemmas and make the best moral decisions for their patients, themselves, and their future colleagues.
